claim: Vinculin regulates cell fate decisions by preventing precocious activation and differentiation of intestinal progenitors into absorptive cells.
source: Using the Drosophila intestinal epithelium, we investigate the role of vinculin, one of the best characterised mechanoeffectors, which functions in both cadherin and integrin adhesion complexes. We discovered that vinculin regulates cell fate decisions, by preventing precocious activation and differentiation of intestinal progenitors into absorptive cells.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that vinculin depletion leads to increased differentiation of enteroblasts into enterocytes, as demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches including RNAi knockdown and mutant analysis.

claim: Vinculin functions in concert with α-catenin at sites of cadherin adhesion rather than as part of integrin function.
source: It achieves this in concert with α-catenin at sites of cadherin adhesion, rather than as part of integrin function.
evidence: The manuscript provides experimental data showing that vinculin's function depends on its interaction with α-catenin, and that α-catenin constructs lacking the vinculin-binding site fail to rescue the phenotype.

claim: Following asymmetric division of the stem cell, vinculin is required only on the enteroblast side to maintain the enteroblast in a quiescent state.
source: Following asymmetric division of the stem cell into a stem cell and an enteroblast (EB), the two cells initially remain connected by adherens junctions, where vinculin is required, only on the EB side, to maintain the EB in a quiescent state and inhibit further divisions of the stem cell.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from cell-specific knockdown experiments showing that vinculin knockdown in EBs, but not ISCs alone, affects tissue homeostasis and differentiation.

claim: Vinculin recruitment to adherens junctions regulates enteroblast activation and numbers through manipulation of cell tension.
source: By manipulating cell tension, we show that vinculin recruitment to adherens junction regulates EB activation and numbers.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that expression of constitutively active myosin II increases vinculin recruitment to junctions, and that altering myosin II activity affects EB differentiation.

claim: Removing vinculin results in an enlarged gut with improved resistance to starvation.
source: Consequently, removing vinculin results in an enlarged gut with improved resistance to starvation.
evidence: The manuscript presents survival data showing that flies with vinculin knockdown in progenitor cells survive starvation better than control flies.

claim: Mechanical regulation at the contact between stem cells and their progeny is used to control tissue cell number.
source: Thus, mechanical regulation at the contact between stem cells and their progeny is used to control tissue cell number.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that vinculin, a mechanosensor, regulates EB differentiation and tissue cell numbers through its function at adherens junctions.

claim: In the mammalian intestine, uncompensated cell loss can result in chronic inflammation.
source: In the intestine for example, where the rate of tissue turnover is high, uncompensated cell loss can result in chronic inflammation, whereas over-proliferation and mis-differentiation can produce adenomas that constitute a sensitised background for tumour initiation (Gehart and Clevers, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gehart and Clevers, 2019.

claim: Over-proliferation and mis-differentiation in the intestine can produce adenomas that constitute a sensitised background for tumour initiation.
source: In the intestine for example, where the rate of tissue turnover is high, uncompensated cell loss can result in chronic inflammation, whereas over-proliferation and mis-differentiation can produce adenomas that constitute a sensitised background for tumour initiation (Gehart and Clevers, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gehart and Clevers, 2019.

claim: In the mammalian intestine, a combination of locally secreted and membrane-bound proteins regulates cell fate decisions across the crypt–villus axis through the activation of key signal transduction pathways, including Wnt and Notch.
source: In the mammalian intestine, a combination of locally secreted and membrane-bound proteins regulates cell fate decisions across the crypt–villus axis through the activation of key signal transduction pathways, including Wnt and Notch (Meran et al., 2017; Gehart and Clevers, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meran et al., 2017 and Gehart and Clevers, 2019.

claim: There is an increased appreciation of a potential role of mechanical cues from surrounding cells in regulating cell fate determination in the intestine.
source: There is also an increased appreciation of a potential role of mechanical cues from surrounding cells – through cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion protein complexes – in regulating cell fate determination, as observed in other systems (Meran et al., 2017; Wickström and Niessen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meran et al., 2017 and Wickström and Niessen, 2018.

claim: Mechanosensing of the extracellular matrix is currently under investigation in intestinal organoid cultures.
source: Although mechanosensing of the extracellular matrix is currently under investigation in intestinal organoid cultures (Gjorevski et al., 2016), the regulation of intestinal cell fate by adhesion complexes is in general poorly understood compared to canonical signalling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gjorevski et al., 2016.

claim: The regulation of intestinal cell fate by adhesion complexes is poorly understood compared to canonical signalling pathways.
source: Although mechanosensing of the extracellular matrix is currently under investigation in intestinal organoid cultures (Gjorevski et al., 2016), the regulation of intestinal cell fate by adhesion complexes is in general poorly understood compared to canonical signalling pathways.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by the context of existing research.

claim: Transmembrane E-cadherin proteins engage in homophilic adhesion via their extracellular domain.
source: At adherens junctions between neighbouring epithelial cells, transmembrane E-cadherin proteins engage in homophilic adhesion via their extracellular domain, and indirectly associate with the cytoskeleton by the recruitment of β-catenin via their intracellular domain, which can interact with various actin-binding proteins including α-catenin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E-cadherin structure and function.

claim: E-cadherin indirectly associates with the cytoskeleton by the recruitment of β-catenin via their intracellular domain, which can interact with various actin-binding proteins including α-catenin.
source: At adherens junctions between neighbouring epithelial cells, transmembrane E-cadherin proteins engage in homophilic adhesion via their extracellular domain, and indirectly associate with the cytoskeleton by the recruitment of β-catenin via their intracellular domain, which can interact with various actin-binding proteins including α-catenin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E-cadherin adhesion complex.

claim: Heterodimeric transmembrane proteins integrins and their associated proteins, including talin, contribute to focal adhesions at cell–matrix junctions, linking extracellular ligands to cytoskeletal proteins.
source: Heterodimeric transmembrane proteins integrins and their associated proteins, including talin, contribute to focal adhesions at cell–matrix junctions, thus linking extracellular ligands to cytoskeletal proteins (Hynes, 2002; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hynes, 2002 and Sun et al., 2016.

claim: Genetic ablation of integrins in intestinal stem cells prevents overproliferation following over-activation of growth factor signalling pathways in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila for example, genetic ablation of integrins in intestinal stem cells (ISCs) prevents overproliferation following over-activation of growth factor signalling pathways (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Why integrins are required for proliferation in the Drosophila intestine remains unsolved.
source: However, why integrins are required for proliferation remains unsolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Vinculin is capable of stabilising both adherens junctions and focal adhesions under tension.
source: One candidate of interest is the highly conserved actin-binding protein vinculin, as it is capable of stabilising both adherens junctions and focal adhesions under tension (Bays and DeMali, 2017) and of regulating cell fate decisions in cell culture models and in vivo in the mouse skin (Holle et al., 2013; Kuroda et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Biswas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bays and DeMali, 2017.

claim: Vinculin is capable of regulating cell fate decisions in cell culture models and in vivo in the mouse skin.
source: One candidate of interest is the highly conserved actin-binding protein vinculin, as it is capable of stabilising both adherens junctions and focal adhesions under tension (Bays and DeMali, 2017) and of regulating cell fate decisions in cell culture models and in vivo in the mouse skin (Holle et al., 2013; Kuroda et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Biswas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Holle et al., 2013; Kuroda et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Biswas et al., 2021.

claim: Vinculin protein consists of a head and a tail domain separated by a linker region.
source: Vinculin protein consists of a head and a tail domain separated by a linker region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vinculin protein structure.

claim: In cells, vinculin transits from a closed, auto-inhibited inactive conformation to an open, active conformation initiated by force-dependent protein unfolding.
source: In cells, vinculin transits from a closed, auto-inhibited inactive conformation (whereby the head and tail domains interact with each other, preventing further protein–protein interactions), to an open, active conformation initiated by force-dependent protein unfolding (reviewed in Carisey and Ballestrem, 2011; Bays and DeMali, 2017), that enables the vinculin tail domain to bind F-actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carisey and Ballestrem, 2011 and Bays and DeMali, 2017.

claim: The open, active conformation of vinculin enables the vinculin tail domain to bind F-actin.
source: In cells, vinculin transits from a closed, auto-inhibited inactive conformation (whereby the head and tail domains interact with each other, preventing further protein–protein interactions), to an open, active conformation initiated by force-dependent protein unfolding (reviewed in Carisey and Ballestrem, 2011; Bays and DeMali, 2017), that enables the vinculin tail domain to bind F-actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carisey and Ballestrem, 2011 and Bays and DeMali, 2017.

claim: The vinculin head domain can bind vinculin-binding sites (VBS) present in other proteins including α-catenin and talin.
source: The head domain can bind vinculin-binding sites (VBS) present in other proteins (including α-catenin and talin).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vinculin protein interactions.

claim: Intracellular tension induces conformational changes in α-catenin and talin, exposing their cryptic VBS and initiating vinculin binding.
source: Notably, intracellular tension induces conformational changes in α-catenin and talin, exposing their cryptic VBS and initiating vinculin binding (del Rio et al., 2009; Yonemura et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to del Rio et al., 2009; Yonemura et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2014.

claim: Vinculin binding to α-catenin and talin allows a transition of vinculin into an open conformation able to bind to the actin cytoskeleton, enabling adhesion complexes to withstand higher forces in cells under tension.
source: This allows a transition of vinculin into an open conformation able to bind to the actin cytoskeleton, in turn enabling adhesion complexes to withstand higher forces in cells under tension (le Duc et al., 2010; Dumbauld et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to le Duc et al., 2010; Dumbauld et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2013.

claim: Vinculin is one of the best characterised mechanoeffectors, as mechanical force on both talin and α-catenin is converted into differential vinculin recruitment.
source: Thus, vinculin is one of the best characterised mechanoeffectors, as mechanical force on both talin and α-catenin is converted into differential vinculin recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the established knowledge about vinculin's mechanosensitive properties.

claim: Loss of vinculin is embryonic lethal in mice due to defects in neural tube closure and heart development.
source: In vivo, loss of vinculin is embryonic lethal in mice due to defects in neural tube closure and heart development (Xu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 1998.

claim: Loss of vinculin in Drosophila is homozygous viable and fertile.
source: In Drosophila, loss of vinculin is homozygous viable and fertile (Alatortsev et al., 1997; Klapholz et al., 2015), precluding an essential role during embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alatortsev et al., 1997 and Klapholz et al., 2015.

claim: Vinculin does not have an essential role during embryonic development in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, loss of vinculin is homozygous viable and fertile (Alatortsev et al., 1997; Klapholz et al., 2015), precluding an essential role during embryonic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that vinculin mutants are viable and fertile.

claim: In post-embryonic muscles, Drosophila vinculin regulates actin organisation at integrin junctions.
source: In post-embryonic muscles, Drosophila vinculin regulates actin organisation at integrin junctions (Bharadwaj et al., 2013; Green et al., 2018), and is lethal if expressed in a constitutively active form (Maartens et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bharadwaj et al., 2013 and Green et al., 2018.

claim: Expression of constitutively active vinculin is lethal in Drosophila.
source: In post-embryonic muscles, Drosophila vinculin regulates actin organisation at integrin junctions (Bharadwaj et al., 2013; Green et al., 2018), and is lethal if expressed in a constitutively active form (Maartens et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maartens et al., 2016.

claim: In Drosophila epithelia, vinculin contributes to myosin II mediated tension sensing at cell–cell junctions through its interaction with α-catenin.
source: In epithelia, Drosophila vinculin contributes to myosin II mediated tension sensing at cell–cell junctions through its interaction with α-catenin (Case et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2016; Kale et al., 2018; Alégot et al., 2019), with functions at integrin adhesion sites in epithelia remaining to be identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Case et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2016; Kale et al., 2018; Alégot et al., 2019.

claim: Functions of vinculin at integrin adhesion sites in Drosophila epithelia remain to be identified.
source: In epithelia, Drosophila vinculin contributes to myosin II mediated tension sensing at cell–cell junctions through its interaction with α-catenin (Case et al., 2015; Jurado et al., 2016; Kale et al., 2018; Alégot et al., 2019), with functions at integrin adhesion sites in epithelia remaining to be identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Conditional vinculin knock-out in the mouse skin epidermis revealed a dispensable role in reinforcing newly formed adherens junctions in the stratified epidermis.
source: Conditional vinculin knock-out in the mouse skin epidermis revealed a dispensable role in reinforcing newly formed adherens junctions in the stratified epidermis (Rübsam et al., 2017), and a more prominent role in maintaining stem cells in a quiescent state via stabilisation of adherens junctions and contact inhibition in the hair follicle bulge (Biswas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rübsam et al., 2017.

claim: Vinculin has a role in maintaining stem cells in a quiescent state via stabilisation of adherens junctions and contact inhibition in the mouse hair follicle bulge.
source: Conditional vinculin knock-out in the mouse skin epidermis revealed a dispensable role in reinforcing newly formed adherens junctions in the stratified epidermis (Rübsam et al., 2017), and a more prominent role in maintaining stem cells in a quiescent state via stabilisation of adherens junctions and contact inhibition in the hair follicle bulge (Biswas et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas et al., 2021.

claim: The variety of phenotypes observed for vinculin among different tissues and organisms suggest that vinculin functions in a highly context-specific manner.
source: The variety of phenotypes observed so far among different tissues and organisms suggest that vinculin functions in a highly context-specific manner, and thus, characterising its contribution to tissue homeostasis in multiple systems is required to improve our understanding of mechanotransduction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diverse phenotypes described in the literature.

claim: The role of vinculin in epithelial maintenance and stem cell lineage decisions is unknown in the intestine.
source: The role of vinculin in epithelial maintenance and stem cell lineage decisions is unknown in the intestine.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, which motivates the current study.

claim: Upon cell division in the Drosophila intestine, ISCs self-renew and produce precursor cells able to differentiate into either secretory enteroendocrine cells (EEs) or large absorptive enterocytes (ECs).
source: Upon cell division, ISCs self-renew and produce precursor cells able to differentiate into either secretory enteroendocrine cells (EEs) or large absorptive enterocytes (ECs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006 and Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Drosophila ISCs and their undifferentiated daughter cells, enteroblasts (EBs), are collectively called progenitor cells and express the transcription factor escargot (esg).
source: Drosophila ISCs and their undifferentiated daughter cells, enteroblasts (EBs), are collectively called progenitor cells and express the transcription factor escargot (esg) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila intestinal stem cell biology, supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: As EBs differentiate into ECs, cells develop membrane protrusions and adopt a migratory phenotype, allowing them to move between cells.
source: As EBs differentiate into ECs, through changes in gene expression, cells develop membrane protrusions and adopt a migratory phenotype, allowing them to move between cells; EBs also progressively increase in cell volume, resulting in an extended contact area on the basal side (Antonello et al., 2015; Rojas Villa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antonello et al., 2015 and Rojas Villa et al., 2019.

claim: EBs progressively increase in cell volume during differentiation into ECs, resulting in an extended contact area on the basal side.
source: As EBs differentiate into ECs, through changes in gene expression, cells develop membrane protrusions and adopt a migratory phenotype, allowing them to move between cells; EBs also progressively increase in cell volume, resulting in an extended contact area on the basal side (Antonello et al., 2015; Rojas Villa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antonello et al., 2015 and Rojas Villa et al., 2019.

claim: In the Drosophila intestine, loss of integrin-mediated adhesion has deleterious effects on stem cell maintenance and proliferation.
source: In the Drosophila intestine, loss of integrin-mediated adhesion has deleterious effects on stem cell maintenance and proliferation (Goulas et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013; Okumura et al., 2014; You et al., 2014) and E-cadherin-mediated adhesion regulates stem cell maintenance and differentiation (Choi et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goulas et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013; Okumura et al., 2014; You et al., 2014.

claim: E-cadherin-mediated adhesion regulates stem cell maintenance and differentiation in the Drosophila intestine.
source: In the Drosophila intestine, loss of integrin-mediated adhesion has deleterious effects on stem cell maintenance and proliferation (Goulas et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013; Okumura et al., 2014; You et al., 2014) and E-cadherin-mediated adhesion regulates stem cell maintenance and differentiation (Choi et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2017.

claim: Gut regions R4 and R5 are reduced by RNAi knockdown of talin but not vinculin.
source: Gut regions R4 and R5 are reduced by RNAi knockdown of talin but not vinculin, green fluorescent protein (GFP; green) marks cells expressing the RNAi, and nuclei are blue (DAPI, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: RNAi knockdown of integrin and talin shows reduced number of RNAi-expressing ISC/EB cells and their rounded morphology.
source: RNAi knockdown of integrin and talin shows reduced number of RNAi-expressing ISC/EB cells (GFP+) and their rounded morphology (insets).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: There are more ISC/EB cells in the absence of vinculin and they are enlarged.
source: In contrast there are more ISC/EB cells in the absence of vinculin and they are enlarged.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: Vinculin knockdown in ISCs and EBs results in an overall change in total cell density.
source: These changes result in an overall change in total cell density (F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Vinculin is expressed ubiquitously in the Drosophila gut and localises to cell–matrix and cell–cell junctions.
source: Vinculin, which is expressed ubiquitously in the gut and localises to cell–matrix and cell–cell junctions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F), has not been characterised in the adult intestine.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Expression of two different validated RNAi lines against vinculin did not impact gut length and instead led to an increase in GFP+ cells number and total cell density.
source: Expression of two different validated RNAi lines against vinculin (vinc) did not impact gut length and instead led to an increase in GFP+ cells number and total cell density (Figure 1B–F), associated with increased proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Vinculin knockdown in progenitor cells is associated with increased proliferation.
source: Expression of two different validated RNAi lines against vinculin (vinc) did not impact gut length and instead led to an increase in GFP+ cells number and total cell density (Figure 1B–F), associated with increased proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The intestines of vinc102.1 mutants were wider compared to control yw flies, despite being of comparable lengths.
source: After dissection, we noted that the intestines of vinc102.1 mutants were wider compared to control yw flies, despite being of comparable lengths.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The adult wing surface areas of yw and vinc102.1 flies are comparable.
source: We tested if the difference in gut width reflected a gross difference in body size by measuring the adult wing surface areas of yw and vinc102.1 flies. As we found them to be comparable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and in accordance with (Sarpal et al., 2019), we next set out to establish if the increased gut width resulted from an increase in cell numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Sarpal et al., 2019.

claim: vinc102.1 gut cross-sections had approximately twice as many cells as yw guts when comparing guts of similar width.
source: Importantly, even when we compared guts of similar width (between 190 and 220 μm in Figure 2B), we found that vinc102.1 gut cross-sections had approximately twice as many cells as yw guts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A large GFP+ region is present in the R4/5 region of vinc102.1 esgts F/O guts 14 days after induction of Gal4 expression.
source: Left panels: progenitors and newly produced cells (GFP+, green) 14 days after induction of Gal4 expression. A large GFP+ region is present in the R4/5 region of vinc102.1 esgts F/O guts.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The distribution of newly produced cells was largely uniform and low across the posterior midguts of yw flies.
source: Whereas the distribution of newly produced cells was largely uniform and low across the posterior midguts of yw flies (Figure 2D, top panel), guts of vinc102.1 flies presented with a strong labelling at the interface between R4/5 regions of the posterior midgut (regions defined in Buchon et al., 2013; Figure 2D middle panel, compare to cartoon Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to Buchon et al., 2013.

claim: Guts of vinc102.1 flies presented with a strong labelling at the interface between R4/5 regions of the posterior midgut.
source: Whereas the distribution of newly produced cells was largely uniform and low across the posterior midguts of yw flies (Figure 2D, top panel), guts of vinc102.1 flies presented with a strong labelling at the interface between R4/5 regions of the posterior midgut (regions defined in Buchon et al., 2013; Figure 2D middle panel, compare to cartoon Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to Buchon et al., 2013.

claim: The vinc102.1 phenotype of increased tissue turnover was fully rescued in flies carrying a genomic vinc rescue construct (Vinc-RFP).
source: The phenotype was fully rescued in flies carrying a genomic vinc rescue construct (Vinc-RFP, Klapholz et al., 2015) (n = 34, Figure 2D, bottom panel), confirming that it is vinc loss that accelerates tissue turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to Klapholz et al., 2015.

claim: The increase in cells observed when vinculin is removed indicates that vinculin inhibits cell renewal under basal conditions.
source: Altogether, the increase in cells observed when vinculin is removed indicates that vinculin inhibits cell renewal under basal conditions (locally and possibly through tissue interactions).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased cell numbers in vinculin mutants.

claim: Unlike vinc knockdown in both ISCs and EBs, vinc knockdown in ISCs only did not detect any change in stem cell proportion or tissue density.
source: Unlike vinc knockdown in both ISCs and EBs, we did not detect any change in stem cell proportion or tissue density (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: mys or talin knockdown in ISCs led to a clear rounding and detachment of ISCs from the basement membrane as seen by the delocalisation of β-catenin to the basal side of the cell.
source: This was again in contrast to mys or talin knockdown that led to a clear rounding and detachment of ISCs from the basement membrane as seen by the delocalisation of β-catenin to the basal side of the cell (Figure 3A, orthogonal views), possibly explaining the significant reduction of the stem cell population (Figure 3B) and cell density (Figure 3C) not observed with ISC-specific vinc knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mys or talin knockdown in ISCs resulted in a significant reduction of the stem cell population and cell density.
source: This was again in contrast to mys or talin knockdown that led to a clear rounding and detachment of ISCs from the basement membrane as seen by the delocalisation of β-catenin to the basal side of the cell (Figure 3A, orthogonal views), possibly explaining the significant reduction of the stem cell population (Figure 3B) and cell density (Figure 3C) not observed with ISC-specific vinc knockdown.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: vinc102.1 guts had a clear accumulation of NRE-lacZ+ cells, especially in the region of high turnover R4/5.
source: vinc102.1 guts had a clear accumulation of NRE-lacZ+ cells (especially in the region of high turnover R4/5 marked with longitudinal arrows in the vinc102.1 gut in Figure 4A), and the overall proportion of stem cells was reduced (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The overall proportion of stem cells was reduced in vinc102.1 guts.
source: vinc102.1 guts had a clear accumulation of NRE-lacZ+ cells (especially in the region of high turnover R4/5 marked with longitudinal arrows in the vinc102.1 gut in Figure 4A), and the overall proportion of stem cells was reduced (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In control tissues, EBs were distributed in two groups, with dormant and activated cells corresponding to smaller and bigger nuclei/cells, respectively.
source: In control tissues, EBs were distributed in two groups (see yw violin plots, Figure 4D), with dormant and activated cells corresponding to smaller and bigger nuclei/cells, respectively (Antonello et al., 2015; Rojas Villa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and citations to Antonello et al., 2015 and Rojas Villa et al., 2019.

claim: The large majority of vinc102.1 EBs had bigger nuclei, suggesting reduced numbers of cells were in the dormant stage in the absence of vinc.
source: In contrast, the large majority of vinc102.1 EBs had bigger nuclei, suggesting reduced numbers of cells were in the dormant stage in the absence of vinc.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Most ECs in vinc102.1 guts had smaller nuclei compared to yw guts, suggesting incomplete maturation of ECs.
source: We also noted that most ECs in vinc102.1 guts had smaller nuclei compared to yw guts, suggesting incomplete maturation of ECs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There were no differences in overall clone size between control, vinc102.1 mutant or vinc-RNAi-expressing clones, indicating that similar numbers of cells were produced from a single stem cell.
source: We did not detect differences in overall clone size, indicating that similar numbers of cells were produced from a single stem cell (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The proportion of Dl+ ISCs was reduced in vinc102.1 mutant or vinc-RNAi-expressing clones.
source: We noted however that the proportion of Dl+ ISCs was reduced in vinc102.1 mutant or vinc-RNAi-expressing clones (Figure 4E, F), with some clones devoid of Dl staining (see Zooms in Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E, F.

claim: Despite having fewer stem cells in the absence of vinculin, clones can grow to comparable sizes to control clones, indicating stem cells must have divided more frequently.
source: Thus, despite having fewer stem cells in the absence of vinculin, clones can grow to comparable sizes to control clones, indicating stem cells must have divided more frequently.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that clone sizes are similar despite reduced ISC numbers.

claim: The presence of clones devoid of Dl+ stem cells supports the possibility that mitotic events producing two differentiated daughter cells may occur more frequently in the absence of vinculin.
source: The presence of clones devoid of Dl+ stem cells supports the possibility that mitotic events producing two differentiated daughter cells may occur more frequently in the absence of vinculin, as suggested from data in vinc homozygous tissues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of clones lacking ISCs.

claim: Vinculin might control EB numbers, at the expense of the ISC population.
source: As the clones contained comparable proportions of EEs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), but higher ratios of cells with bigger nuclei (indicative of EB maturation, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), it suggested that vinculin might control EB numbers, at the expense of the ISC population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clone composition data.

claim: Vinculin in EB cell autonomously controls differentiation, and non-cell autonomously regulate ISC proliferation.
source: Together with our previous results showing that stem cell divisions increase upon vinc knockdown in ISCs+EBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), but that vinc knockdown in ISCs had no effect (Figure 3), we hypothesised that vinculin in EB cell autonomously controls differentiation, and non-cell autonomously regulate ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the combined results from multiple experiments.

claim: vincRNAi expression in esg+ cells led to faster progenitor differentiation cells.
source: vincRNAi expression in esg+ cells led to faster progenitor differentiation cells (Figure 5A–C; note the accumulation of GFP−RFP+ cells) and an increased differentiation index calculated as the ratio of GFP−RFP+ cells/total cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Expression of vincRNAi in klu+ cells confirmed a role of vinculin in EBs to control their production.
source: Expression of vincRNAi in klu+ cells confirmed a role of vinculin in EBs to control their production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and to indirectly regulate proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) and cell density (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Instances of mitotic EBs (PH3+ Klu+ cells) were observed following vincRNAi expression.
source: Occasionally, we observed instances of mitotic EBs (PH3+ Klu+ cells) following vincRNAi expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The abnormal occurrence of mitotic marker in EB cells suggests these newly generated EBs have kept some mitotic potential.
source: This abnormal occurrence of mitotic marker in EB cells, which are normally post-mitotic, suggests these newly generated EBs have kept some mitotic potential.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of mitotic markers in EBs.

claim: Vinculin knockdown in ECs did not affect cell density.
source: In contrast to vinculin knockdown in EBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), knockdown in ECs did not affect cell density (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that vinculin acts specifically in EBs to maintain them in a dormant state to tune differentiation rates to tissue needs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vinculin acts specifically in EBs to maintain them in a dormant state to tune differentiation rates to tissue needs.
source: In contrast to vinculin knockdown in EBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), knockdown in ECs did not affect cell density (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that vinculin acts specifically in EBs to maintain them in a dormant state to tune differentiation rates to tissue needs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell-type specific knockdown experiments.

claim: Adherens junctions between dormant EBs and ISCs regulate ISC proliferation.
source: Adherens junctions between dormant EBs and ISCs regulate ISC proliferation (Choi et al., 2011; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2011 and Zhai et al., 2017.

claim: Vinculin was present in adherens junctions, co-localising with β-catenin.
source: We found that vinculin was present in adherens junctions, co-localising with β-catenin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: α-cat RNAi expression resulted in larger esg+ cells, equivalent in size to differentiating EBs and ECs.
source: Nuclear size quantification of GFP+ progenitor cells showed that as in vincRNAi-expressing guts, α-cat RNAi expression resulted in larger esg+ cells, equivalent in size to differentiating EBs and ECs (Figure 6B) and an overall accumulation of progenitors (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: α-cat RNAi expression resulted in an overall accumulation of progenitors.
source: Nuclear size quantification of GFP+ progenitor cells showed that as in vincRNAi-expressing guts, α-cat RNAi expression resulted in larger esg+ cells, equivalent in size to differentiating EBs and ECs (Figure 6B) and an overall accumulation of progenitors (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of vinc did not alter α-catenin membrane localisation.
source: Consistent with being downstream of α-catenin, knockdown of vinc did not alter α-catenin membrane localisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but knockdown of α-catenin reduced vinculin recruitment to adherens junctions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of α-catenin reduced vinculin recruitment to adherens junctions.
source: Consistent with being downstream of α-catenin, knockdown of vinc did not alter α-catenin membrane localisation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), but knockdown of α-catenin reduced vinculin recruitment to adherens junctions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: α-catenin is required upstream of vinculin in progenitor cells to regulate tissue turnover.
source: Thus, α-catenin is required upstream of vinculin in progenitor cells to regulate tissue turnover.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that α-catenin knockdown reduces vinculin recruitment and produces similar phenotypes to vinculin knockdown.

claim: Guts rescued by co-expression of full-length α-catenin (α-Cat FL) were indistinguishable from wild-type controls, with similar rates of differentiation.
source: Guts rescued by co-expression of full-length α-catenin (α-Cat FL) were indistinguishable from wild-type controls (expression of ReDDM only in esg+), with similar rates of differentiation (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: Co-expression of α-catenin constructs with the VBS deleted (α-Cat ΔM1a and ΔM1b) failed to rescue EBs accumulation.
source: In contrast, co-expression of α-catenin constructs with the VBS deleted (α-Cat ΔM1a and ΔM1b), failed to rescue EBs accumulation (although intriguingly, we noted a milder phenotype with α-Cat ΔM1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: Deleting the adjacent M2 domain did not impair the ability of α-catenin to rescue the vinculin phenotype.
source: Deleting the adjacent M2 domain did not impair the ability of α-catenin to rescue this phenotype (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: The absence of VBS in α-catenin has no effect in ISCs but promotes EB differentiation and increase in numbers.
source: We next tested the role of the vinculin/α-catenin interaction in ISCs or EBs by co-expressing α-Cat RNAi and α-Cat ΔM1a and observed that the absence of VBS in α-catenin has no effect in ISCs but promotes EB differentiation and increase in numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vinculin represses activation of a pool of EC precursors via its interaction with α-catenin.
source: We conclude that vinculin represses activation of a pool of EC precursors via its interaction with α-catenin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with α-catenin constructs.

claim: EB-specific knockdown of E-cadherin (Drosophila shotgun, shg) and α-catenin triggered faster differentiation.
source: In support of this model, EB-specific knockdown of E-cadherin (Drosophila shotgun, shg) and α-catenin triggered faster differentiation (shown after 3 days of RNAi expression in Figure 6—figure supplement 3, as longer expression with Klu-Gal4 compromised fly survival).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Integrin and talin also contribute to EB differentiation.
source: Since vinculin could in principle have a role at both cell–cell and cell–matrix adhesion sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F), we also tested the role of integrin-mediated adhesion in EBs and found that integrin and talin also contribute to EB differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both adhesion machineries (cell-cell and cell-matrix) are required in the EB–EC differentiation step, with a clear role for vinculin/α-catenin in EBs only, and additional roles for integrin/talin in ISC maintenance.
source: Thus, both adhesion machineries are required in the EB–EC differentiation step, with a clear role for vinculin/α-catenin in EBs only, and additional roles for integrin/talin in ISC maintenance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of knockdown experiments in different cell types.

claim: Expression of a phospho-mimetic, active, form of Sqh for 14 days resulted in small round progenitor cells that remained undifferentiated in control guts.
source: The activity of myosin II can be elevated experimentally by expression of a phospho-mimetic, active, form of Sqh (Mitonaka et al., 2007). Expression for 14 days resulted in small round progenitor cells (similar to dormant EBs described in Rojas Villa et al., 2019), that remained undifferentiated in control guts (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and citations to Mitonaka et al., 2007 and Rojas Villa et al., 2019.

claim: RNAi-mediated downregulation of sqh or zip mildly increased differentiation rates.
source: Instead, RNAi-mediated downregulation of sqh or zip (predicted to reduce cell contractility) mildly increased differentiation rates, and many EBs cells changed shape and were visibly more advanced towards EC differentiation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), reminiscent of the semi-differentiated status of vincRNAi-expressing EBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Altering cell contractility directly impacts progenitor differentiation.
source: These results show that altering cell contractility directly impacts progenitor differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myosin II manipulation experiments.

claim: Expression of SqhDD in vinc102.1 progenitor cells did not prevent the accelerated differentiation, suggesting that vinculin acts downstream of cellular contractility to regulate tissue turnover.
source: Expression of SqhDD in vinc102.1 progenitor cells did not prevent the accelerated differentiation (Figure 7A, B), suggesting that vinculin acts downstream of cellular contractility to regulate tissue turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Increased vinculin recruitment to EB adherens junctions was observed when SqhDD was expressed in these cells.
source: As we also observed increased vinculin recruitment to EB adherens junctions when SqhDD was expressed in these cells (Figure 7C, D), we concluded that vinculin functions downstream of cortical tension, and is mechanosensitive like in other tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C, D.

claim: Vinculin functions downstream of cortical tension, and is mechanosensitive like in other tissues.
source: As we also observed increased vinculin recruitment to EB adherens junctions when SqhDD was expressed in these cells (Figure 7C, D), we concluded that vinculin functions downstream of cortical tension, and is mechanosensitive like in other tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vinculin recruitment data upon myosin II activation.

claim: A constitutively open form of vinculin slowed down tissue turnover in vinc102.1 guts.
source: In addition, we observed that a constitutively open form of vinculin (Maartens et al., 2016) slowed down tissue turnover in vinc102.1 guts (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Maartens et al., 2016.

claim: Vinculin associates with the VBS of α-catenin in EBs, which becomes exposed upon force-induced α-catenin conformational change, and this binding prevents premature EB differentiation and increased ISC proliferation.
source: Altogether, our data support a model whereby vinculin associates with the VBS of α-catenin in EBs, which becomes exposed upon force-induced α-catenin conformational change. This binding prevents premature EB differentiation and increased ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined experimental data.

claim: The idea that vinculin functions by mediating increased tension on adherens junction was supported by the effects of independently altering acto-myosin function.
source: The idea that vinculin functions by mediating increased tension on adherens junction was supported by the effects of independently altering acto-myosin function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the myosin II manipulation experiments.

claim: Plasticity is an important component of intestinal function with stem cell proliferation and progenitor differentiation able to transiently alter in response to diet and regenerate tissue after damage, before reverting to steady-state levels.
source: Our experiments have focussed on the gut in a homeostatic state, however plasticity is an important component of intestinal function with stem cell proliferation and progenitor differentiation able to transiently alter in response to diet and regenerate tissue after damage, before reverting to steady-state levels (e.g. Buchon et al., 2010; O'Brien et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buchon et al., 2010 and O'Brien et al., 2011.

claim: Starvation results in cell depletion and gut shortening in Drosophila, whilst refeeding induces cell proliferation and gut growth.
source: To test this, we subjected flies to a cycle of starvation and refeeding as starvation results in cell depletion and gut shortening, whilst refeeding induces cell proliferation and gut growth (McLeod et al., 2010; O'Brien et al., 2011; Lucchetta and Ohlstein, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLeod et al., 2010; O'Brien et al., 2011; Lucchetta and Ohlstein, 2017.

claim: Both yw and vinc102.1 genotypes showed expected reversible changes in gut width and length during starvation and refeeding, indicating that vinculin is dispensable for diet-induced tissue clearance and repopulation.
source: We observed expected reversible changes in gut width and length (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D) for both genotypes, indicating that vinculin is dispensable for diet-induced tissue clearance and repopulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: vinc102.1 flies showed better survival to the starvation regime compared to yw flies.
source: However, vinc102.1 flies showed better survival to the starvation regime compared to yw flies (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Flies with vincRNAi expressed in adult intestinal progenitor cells showed better survival during starvation.
source: As this improved resilience to starvation could be a result of vinculin loss in the gut or other tissues, we compared the survival of starved flies when vincRNAi was expressed in adult intestinal progenitor cells. Again, we observed better survival in the absence of vinculin (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: The larger number of progenitor cells resulting from vinculin depletion could have minimised the deleterious effects of cell loss and/or provided a greater pool of cells ready to start differentiating in the right nutritional conditions.
source: We propose that the larger number of progenitor cells resulting from vinculin depletion could have minimised the deleterious effects of cell loss and/or provided a greater pool of cells ready to start differentiating in the right nutritional conditions.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the improved starvation survival.

claim: Vinculin may play important roles in other tissues to regulate organismal physiology throughout development and adulthood.
source: Whilst we cannot exclude that vinculin may play important roles in other tissues to regulate organismal physiology throughout development and adulthood, our result shows an important contribution of vinculin in progenitor cells to adult fly survival.
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging potential roles of vinculin in other tissues.

claim: Vinculin in progenitor cells makes an important contribution to adult fly survival.
source: Whilst we cannot exclude that vinculin may play important roles in other tissues to regulate organismal physiology throughout development and adulthood, our result shows an important contribution of vinculin in progenitor cells to adult fly survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the starvation survival experiments.

claim: In response to poor nutritional conditions, adherens junctions between ISCs and newly formed EBs were stabilised and stem cell proliferation was prevented.
source: Previous work showed that in response to poor nutritional conditions (or insulin signalling pathway impairment), adherens junctions between ISCs and newly formed EBs were stabilised and stem cell proliferation was prevented (Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Choi et al., 2011.

claim: α-catenin recruitment of active vinculin might help strengthen adherens junctions when cells are under external tension, as would be the case during periods of active growth.
source: Although the signals linking insulin signalling to junction disassembly and non-autonomous proliferation remain to be characterised, it is tempting to speculate that α-catenin recruitment of active vinculin might help strengthen adherens junctions when cells are under external tension, as would be the case during periods of active growth.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of vinculin in response to growth signals.

claim: Upon refeeding after a week of starvation, vinc102.1 guts showed a recovery in size that initially surpassed the original one, correlating with increased cell production facilitated by junction disassembly.
source: In support of this hypothesis, upon refeeding (and thus active insulin signalling) after a week of starvation, vinc102.1 guts showed a recovery in size that initially surpassed the original one, correlating with increased cell production facilitated by junction disassembly.
evidence: This is an observation from the starvation/refeeding experiments that supports the proposed hypothesis.

claim: E-cadherin-mediated cell adhesion is required in ECs to prevent stem cell renewal by preventing the secretion of mitogenic signals.
source: Notably, E-cadherin-mediated cell adhesion is also required in ECs to prevent stem cell renewal, but in this case, by preventing the secretion of mitogenic signals (Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2017.

claim: Coupling of differentiated cell density and self-renewal was demonstrated in vivo in the mouse adult stratified epidermis, where stem cells divide in response to delamination.
source: Such coupling of differentiated cell density and self-renewal was also demonstrated in vivo in the mouse adult stratified epidermis, where stem cells divide in response to delamination (Mesa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mesa et al., 2018.

claim: Regional differences in the rate of tissue turnover were observed in the posterior midgut of vinc102.1 guts.
source: Strikingly, we observed regional differences in the rate of tissue turnover in the posterior midgut of vinc102.1 guts.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The region with highest turnover in the vinc102.1 mutant corresponded to a narrowing portion of the gut where the domains R4 and R5 are separated by a constriction of the intestinal wall.
source: As the region with highest turnover in the mutant corresponded to a narrowing portion of the gut where the domains R4 and R5 are separated by a constriction of the intestinal wall (cartoon Figure 1B, Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), we speculate that a local increase in mechanical forces (e.g. through visceral muscle contractions and food passage) induces vinculin mediated junction reinforcement to prevent untimely cell production.
evidence: This is an observation supported by citations to Buchon et al., 2013 and Marianes and Spradling, 2013.

claim: A local increase in mechanical forces induces vinculin mediated junction reinforcement to prevent untimely cell production.
source: As the region with highest turnover in the mutant corresponded to a narrowing portion of the gut where the domains R4 and R5 are separated by a constriction of the intestinal wall (cartoon Figure 1B, Buchon et al., 2013; Marianes and Spradling, 2013), we speculate that a local increase in mechanical forces (e.g. through visceral muscle contractions and food passage) induces vinculin mediated junction reinforcement to prevent untimely cell production.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism underlying regional differences in turnover.

claim: β-catenin had a stronger cortical localisation in the R4/5 area compared to more anterior areas of the midgut.
source: Consistent with this, β-catenin had a stronger cortical localisation in this area compared to more anterior areas of the midgut (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation mentioned but not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Vinc knockdown in EBs cells led them to stall half-way through differentiation, whilst triggering proliferation in adjacent ISCs.
source: However, we observed that vinc knockdown in EBs cells led them to stall half-way through differentiation, whilst triggering proliferation in adjacent ISCs.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Vinculin prevents the premature activation of dormant EBs.
source: This suggests that vinculin prevents the premature activation of dormant EBs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that vinculin loss leads to EB activation.

claim: Once past a certain threshold of mechanical force, vinculin might not be sufficient to prevent tissue growth.
source: Once past a certain threshold of mechanical force, vinculin might not be sufficient to prevent tissue growth.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limits of vinculin function.

claim: Vinculin might also contribute to terminal differentiation, either by direct signalling of terminal differentiation or by sensing local tissue density in a similar fashion as contact inhibition.
source: Alternatively, vinculin might also contribute to terminal differentiation, either by direct signalling of terminal differentiation or by sensing local tissue density in a similar fashion as contact inhibition (Alégot et al., 2019; Biswas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to Alégot et al., 2019 and Biswas et al., 2021.

claim: Gut stretching after food ingestion induces proliferation through activation of the YAP/TAZ homolog Yorkie.
source: Indeed, gut stretching after food ingestion induces proliferation through activation of the YAP/TAZ homolog Yorkie. The mechanical stress induces a displacement of the Ste20 kinase Misshapen from the membrane of EBs, thereby relieving interactions with upstream mediators of the Hippo pathway, and thus allowing Yorkie nuclear translocation, activation of target genes and midgut growth (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: Mechanical stress induces a displacement of the Ste20 kinase Misshapen from the membrane of EBs, thereby relieving interactions with upstream mediators of the Hippo pathway, and thus allowing Yorkie nuclear translocation, activation of target genes and midgut growth.
source: Indeed, gut stretching after food ingestion induces proliferation through activation of the YAP/TAZ homolog Yorkie. The mechanical stress induces a displacement of the Ste20 kinase Misshapen from the membrane of EBs, thereby relieving interactions with upstream mediators of the Hippo pathway, and thus allowing Yorkie nuclear translocation, activation of target genes and midgut growth (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: Vinculin contributes to mechanical force sensing in EBs and helps coordinate self-renewal and differentiation into absorptive cells.
source: We suggest that vinculin contributes to mechanical force sensing in EBs and more generally helps coordinate self-renewal and differentiation into absorptive cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: The precursors of EEs can transduce mechanical stress to control differentiation through increased intracellular calcium downstream of the stretch-activated channel piezo expressed in EE precursors.
source: Interestingly, the precursors of EEs can also transduce mechanical stress to control differentiation. In this case, however, cell fate is acquired through increased intracellular calcium downstream of the stretch-activated channel piezo expressed in EE precursors (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2018.

claim: Lineage commitment in the Drosophila intestine depends on mechanosensing pathways specifically active in precursors cells.
source: Thus, lineage commitment in the Drosophila intestine seems to depend on mechanosensing pathways specifically active in precursors cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined evidence about mechanosensing in different progenitor cell types.

claim: Cell type-specific mechanosensing pathways contribute to fine-tuning cell production and tissue composition in the Drosophila intestine.
source: Together with the role of integrin activation in ISCs to regulate self-renewal (this work; Lin et al., 2013), it becomes apparent cell type-specific mechanosensing pathways contribute to fine-tuning cell production and tissue composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data and cited work.

claim: In the mammalian intestine, stem cells are located in crypts whilst progenitors concentrate at the bottom of villi, which are populated by differentiated cells.
source: In the mammalian intestine, stem cells are located in crypts whilst progenitors concentrate at the bottom of villi, which are populated by differentiated cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian intestinal architecture.

claim: Epithelial turnover in the mammalian intestine is dependent on E-cadherin mediated adhesion.
source: Epithelial turnover is dependent on E-cadherin mediated adhesion (Hermiston and Gordon, 1995; Hermiston et al., 1996) and continuous cell migration (Krndija et al., 2019) thus, it is harder to establish if forces contribute to proliferation and lineage commitment or active cell migration (and indirectly self-renewal).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hermiston and Gordon, 1995 and Hermiston et al., 1996.

claim: Epithelial turnover in the mammalian intestine is dependent on continuous cell migration.
source: Epithelial turnover is dependent on E-cadherin mediated adhesion (Hermiston and Gordon, 1995; Hermiston et al., 1996) and continuous cell migration (Krndija et al., 2019) thus, it is harder to establish if forces contribute to proliferation and lineage commitment or active cell migration (and indirectly self-renewal).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krndija et al., 2019.

claim: The mechanoeffector protein vinculin is deregulated in gastrointestinal diseases, with expression levels reduced in colorectal cancers.
source: The mechanoeffector protein vinculin is deregulated in gastrointestinal diseases, with expression levels reduced in colorectal cancers (Goldmann et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017) and auto anti-vinculin antibodies are produced in inflammatory bowel syndrome (Rezaie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldmann et al., 2013 and Li et al., 2017.

claim: Auto anti-vinculin antibodies are produced in inflammatory bowel syndrome.
source: The mechanoeffector protein vinculin is deregulated in gastrointestinal diseases, with expression levels reduced in colorectal cancers (Goldmann et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017) and auto anti-vinculin antibodies are produced in inflammatory bowel syndrome (Rezaie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rezaie et al., 2017.

claim: The use of Drosophila as a model organism has allowed identification of an EB-specific role for vinculin mediated by α-catenin and independent of integrin adhesion.
source: The use of a simpler model organism, with a flat intestinal epithelium where stem cells are dispersed among their progeny (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006) and cell migration is sporadic (Antonello et al., 2015; Martin et al., 2018) has allowed us to identify an EB-specific role for vinculin mediated by α-catenin and independent of integrin adhesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental work, supported by citations describing the Drosophila intestinal system.
